sections.h2: Which Knox County offices handle a property tax bill?
sections.html:
Four offices at the Barbourville courthouse complex touch a Knox County tax bill, and each answers a different question. The assessment comes from the property valuation administrator, the sheriff collects the bill, the county clerk takes over unpaid bills, and the county attorney enforces collection of delinquent ones. The Kentucky Department of Revenue explains that the sheriff is the first official responsible for collecting property tax bills and that the county attorney is the official who enforces delinquent ones.

Knox County offices and phone numbers (source: Kentucky Department for Local Government)
OfficeWhat it handlesPhone
Property valuation administratorAssessed value, exemptions, appeal conferences(606) 546-4113
County sheriffCollecting the current-year bill(606) 546-3181
County clerkRecording deeds, delinquent certificates, filing appeals(606) 546-3568
County attorneyEnforcing delinquent bills(606) 546-9515
Fiscal courtCounty government, 401 Court Square(606) 546-6192

The courthouse is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and the county clerk and circuit clerk offices also open Saturday from 8:30 a.m. to noon. A deed for a Knox County house is filed with the clerk on the first floor of the courthouse.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Knox County?
sections.html:
Knox County sits in the Appalachian region of southeastern Kentucky and covers 388 square miles. Barbourville is the county seat and the largest city, with 3,222 residents at the 2020 census. Corbin lies mostly in Whitley County, and the census-designated places include Artemus and Flat Lick. The county touches Clay, Bell, Whitley and Laurel counties, and U.S. Route 25E links Barbourville to Corbin and to Pineville.

The county was formed on December 19, 1799 from part of Lincoln County. Coal mining drove its economy for generations. Health care and social assistance, retail trade and educational services are now the largest employers. Union Commonwealth University is in Barbourville, and the Daniel Boone Festival fills the town in early October.

The Census Bureau counted 30,193 residents in 2020 and estimated 29,532 for July 2025, a drop of 2.2 percent. Its QuickFacts figures for 2020 to 2024 describe the housing market a seller faces:

  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $118,700.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 65.3 percent, with 11,711 households.
  • Median gross rent: $681.
  • Median household income: $32,527.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: zero.

sections.h2: How is a Knox County assessment set, and how do I appeal it?
sections.html:
The property valuation administrator assesses at fair cash value as of January 1 each year, and the county's PVA site states that no exemption is granted without a formal application. The tax roll then opens for public inspection on the first Monday in May for thirteen days. You may not skip the conference step: a property owner must first meet with the PVA or a deputy before filing an appeal.

After a conference, the appeal goes to the county clerk's office by close of business on the workday following the last inspection day. The local board of assessment appeals meets 25 to 35 days after inspection ends and sits for no more than five days without state approval. The board denies an appeal that arrives without supporting evidence, such as sales of comparable homes, repair estimates, insurance values or listings. An owner who files and then does not appear before the board cannot carry the case on to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

With a median owner-occupied value of $118,700, an assessment that sits well above what similar nearby homes sold for is worth a conference. A house in poor condition should be documented with photos and contractor bids before May.

sections.h2: When are Knox County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Kentucky property taxes are due by December 31 of the assessment year, and the sheriff mails bills just before collection opens. The Department of Revenue notes that collection begins on October 1 or November 1 in most counties. The discount and penalty dates differ by county, so read them off the bill the Knox County Sheriff mails, or call the sheriff at (606) 546-3181.

Collection runs until close of business on April 15, and everything unpaid then moves to the county clerk. The bill is a personal debt of the person who owned the property on the January 1 assessment date, and a lien attaches to property with delinquent taxes. Under KRS 134.420 that lien continues for eleven years regardless of who owns the property, which matters to any buyer.

Cash buyers and closing agents handle a current-year bill as a payoff item. Request the figure from the sheriff before the closing date so the settlement statement shows it correctly.

sections.h2: What happens to an unpaid Knox County bill?
sections.html:
On April 15 the sheriff transfers the bill to the Knox County Clerk, where it becomes a certificate of delinquency with a lien recorded against the parcel. The clerk's website points visitors to a delinquent tax lookup called DTax, and it warns that the clerk alone decides the exact dollar amount due at the time of sale.

The Department of Revenue illustrates the cost of waiting with a $1,000 bill. At the moment of transfer it has grown to $1,254 once a 10 percent penalty, an add-on fee and the sheriff's commission are included. Interest then runs at 1 percent per month, and clerk and county attorney commissions follow. The same illustration shows $1,387.79 due within five business days and $1,659.90 if the bill is paid after advertising in June.

  • The county attorney mails a 30-day notice and, if needed, a second notice within 60 days.
  • A sale must be scheduled 90 to 135 days after transfer, which in a normal-schedule county falls between July 14 and August 28.
  • The clerk advertises the certificates 30 to 45 days before the sale in the local paper and on a county website.
  • A certificate that is not paid by the sale date can be bought by a third party, who then collects from you.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the Kentucky homestead exemption in Knox County?
sections.html:
The Department of Revenue set the maximum homestead exemption at $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 tax periods. To qualify, a person must be at least 65 during the tax period or be classified as totally disabled by a public or private retirement system, and the home must be owned, occupied and maintained as the personal residence on January 1.

The application goes to the Knox County PVA no later than December 31 of the eligible tax year. The county PVA's own website lists the age 65 exemption and the exemption for 100 percent totally disabled owners among the exemptions it administers. Because the amount comes off the assessed value, a Knox County owner with a $118,700 home would be taxed on a lower base. The exemption is for people who live in the home, so heirs who inherit a house they do not occupy should not assume it carries over.

sections.h2: How do property taxes work when a Knox County house sells?
sections.html:
The bill follows the January 1 owner, so a house sold in the spring still produces a tax bill in the seller's name. Closing agents normally prorate the year between buyer and seller on the settlement statement and pay the sheriff from the proceeds. A deed to the new owner must include an in-care-of address for the bill for the year of transfer, under KRS 382.135(1)(d).

Heirs who sell an inherited Knox County house, owners behind on payments, and landlords with a vacant rental often ask whether a direct sale to a cash buyer can wrap up the tax in one closing. It can, as long as the payoff is requested ahead of time: ask the sheriff for the current-year figure, and ask the county clerk for any earlier-year certificate. A seller who has a recorded delinquency should also ask the county attorney's office whether a payment arrangement is in place, since that affects what a title company will clear.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Knox County, Kentucky?
faqs.a: Pay the Knox County Sheriff, who collects the current-year bill; the sheriff's office phone is (606) 546-3181. After April 15 an unpaid bill moves to the county clerk at (606) 546-3568, where it is payable as a delinquent certificate.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Knox County assessment?
faqs.a: Meet with the PVA or a deputy first, then file the appeal with the county clerk by close of business on the workday after the tax roll inspection period ends. The PVA's number is (606) 546-4113. Bring evidence such as comparable sales and repair estimates.

faqs.q: Is there a homestead exemption in Knox County?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled under a retirement system, can subtract up to $49,100 for 2025 and 2026 if they own and live in the home on January 1. Apply to the PVA by December 31.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay my Knox County property tax?
faqs.a: The bill becomes a certificate of delinquency at the clerk's office on April 15 with a lien on the property. Interest accrues at 1 percent per month, commissions and fees are added, and a sale to a third-party purchaser can follow 90 to 135 days after the transfer.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Knox County house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The lien stays with the property, so the payoff is settled at closing from the sale proceeds. Request a written figure from the sheriff for the current year and from the county clerk for any delinquent certificate before you set a closing date.
